passages.t: ‘I will sing of the loving devotion of the LORD forever’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite” (verse 1). The psalm begins with a vow to sing. “I will sing of the loving devotion of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will proclaim Your faithfulness to all generations” (verse 1).

Two words run all through this psalm: loving devotion (hesed) and faithfulness. Both are words for God keeping his promises.

At once the singer names the promise that matters most to him. God says, “I have made a covenant with My chosen one, I have sworn to David My servant” (verse 3). He will set David's family on the throne for all generations (verse 4).

Then comes a hymn to God's greatness. No one in the heavens compares with him (verse 6). “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them” (verse 9). He crushed Rahab, the sea monster (verse 10). He made north and south, and the mountains Tabor and Hermon shout for joy (verse 12). “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne; loving devotion and faithfulness go before You” (verse 14).

The people who know this God are happy (verse 15). And the king belongs to him: “our king to the Holy One of Israel” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Ethan the Ezrahite, like Heman in Psalm 88, is named in the Bible both as a singer in David's day (1 Chronicles 15:19) and as a famous wise man (1 Kings 4:31). Whether that is one Ethan or two is not known.

Israel's neighbours told stories of a storm god who won his throne by beating the sea or a sea monster. The note on Psalm 74 says more. Psalm 89 gives that victory to the LORD. The sea, Rahab and every power in heaven answer to him.

Tabor and Hermon (verse 12) were two well-known mountains in the north of the land. Hermon is the tallest peak in the region.

Notice the build-up. The psalm spends its first half making the promise as strong as it can be. God is mighty, faithful and just, and he has sworn to David. Hold on to that. It is about to be tested.
passages.later: The angel told Mary that God would give her son “the throne of His father David” (Luke 1:32). Revelation calls Jesus “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5). Those words echo this psalm, which calls the moon “a faithful witness in the sky” (verse 37) and promises to make David's heir “the highest of the kings of the earth” (verse 27).
passages.asks:
What do you know about God that you would sing even in a hard time? Psalm 89 begins by setting down what is true before it faces what hurts.

Read verse 14 slowly. Righteousness, justice, loving devotion and faithfulness: that is what God's rule rests on. Hold that up beside the news you read, and beside your own life.

passages.t: The promise to David: ‘I will not lie to David’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm retells God's promise to David at length. “I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him” (verse 20). God will hold him up and defeat his enemies (verses 21 to 23).

David will call God ‘Father’. “He will call to Me, ‘You are my Father, my God, the Rock of my salvation’” (verse 26). God will make him “the highest of the kings of the earth” (verse 27). “I will establish his line forever, his throne as long as the heavens endure” (verse 29).

What if David's sons do wrong? God says he will punish them “with the rod” (verse 32). “But I will not withdraw My loving devotion from him, nor ever betray My faithfulness” (verse 33). “I will not violate My covenant or alter the utterance of My lips” (verse 34).

Then the strongest oath of all. God swears by his own holiness. David's line will last forever, his throne “like the sun, like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky” (verses 36 to 37).
passages.hearers:
This is the promise God gave David through the prophet Nathan, in 2 Samuel 7. There God said of David's son, “I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men” (2 Samuel 7:14). And, “your throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). Psalm 89 sings that promise back, phrase by phrase, and makes it even stronger.

Kings in the ancient world sometimes gave a loyal servant a grant that would pass to his heirs. God's promise to David is like that kind of gift. It was given, not earned. And it planned for failure from the start. Sons who sinned would be punished, but the promise itself would stand.

The sun and moon were the most lasting things anyone could see. To tie the promise to them was to say it would never end.
passages.later:
Jeremiah used the same picture: if the day and the night could be stopped, “then My covenant may also be broken with David My servant” (Jeremiah 33:21).

Peter said that David knew God “had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne” (Acts 2:30). Paul said, “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20).
passages.asks:
Notice that God's promise did not depend on David's sons being good. It planned for their failures. Do you believe God's promises to you depend on how well you do? Psalm 89 says that God's faithfulness is bigger than our failures.

And notice how hard the psalm holds God to his word. You may do that too. Faith does not only accept God's promises. It reminds him of them.

passages.t: ‘But You have rejected’: the promise in ruins, and Book Three ends
passages.happening:
Then everything collapses. “Now, however, You have spurned and rejected him; You are enraged by Your anointed one” (verse 38). “You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust” (verse 39).

The king's walls are broken and his forts are rubble (verse 40). His enemies celebrate (verse 42). “You have ended his splendor and cast his throne to the ground” (verse 44). “You have cut short the days of his youth” (verse 45).

Then the questions. “How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever?” (verse 46). “Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David?” (verse 49).

The psalm gives no answer. It ends with the singer bearing the mockery of God's enemies (verses 50 to 51).

Then comes one more line. “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen” (verse 52). That line closes Book Three of the Psalms.
passages.hearers:
The same God who swore ‘I will not violate My covenant’ (verse 34) is now told, ‘You have renounced the covenant’ (verse 39). The psalm puts the promise and the ruin side by side and does not smooth them over. It is one of the boldest prayers in the Bible.

Many readers connect it with the fall of David's line to Babylon, as the book page's timeline describes. A young king, Jehoiachin, came to the throne at eighteen and was taken away to Babylon after three months (2 Kings 24:8, 15). A few years later Jerusalem fell, and after that no son of David ruled as king in Jerusalem again. Others think of an earlier defeat. The psalm names no king.

Verse 52 is a short blessing, a doxology. Each of the first four books of the Psalms ends with one, as the book page explains. Here it is set right after the unanswered question. Book Three ends with the question still open. The book page says that some readers see Book Four, which opens with a prayer of Moses and sings that the LORD is King, as a kind of answer. That is a reading of the book's order, not something it states.
passages.later:
How does the promise to David stand? Jews and Christians answer differently, and each answer deserves respect, as the book page's part on the king's psalms says.

Many Jewish readers hold that the promise still stands and waits. The Messiah, the anointed son of David, is a human king still to come, who will bring peace to the world. Since the world is not yet at peace, they believe he has not yet come.

Christians hold that the promise came true in Jesus, “a descendant of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3), raised from the dead. Paul quotes God's word, “I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David” (Acts 13:34), and says that God kept it by raising Jesus. On this reading the crown that fell in the dust was given back, but to a king whose throne no army can cast down.

Both communities read Psalm 89 with care. They part over who Jesus is, and that is a real difference.
passages.hard:
Did God break his promise? The psalm itself asks it, and these notes will not pretend the question is easy. Readers have given several answers. The promise itself foresaw punishment for sinful kings (verses 30 to 32). The promise was to David's line, not to every king in it, and the line went on. Jehoiachin was later released and honoured in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27). And, as the passage above says, Jews and Christians see the promise standing in different ways.

But notice that the psalm does not give any of those answers. It leaves the question with God, and blesses him anyway.
passages.asks:
Have you held a promise of God that seemed to fall apart? Psalm 89 shows you what to do with it. Say the promise out loud. Say what has happened. Ask God where his love has gone. And then, if you can, bless him anyway, as the last line does.

That blessing in verse 52 is not a happy ending. It is faith that will not let go of God, even with the question still open.
